extraReferences.title: There's more to the story behind rare glass octopus footage

anatomy.lede: Joubin's 1918 drawing shows a female from below: a glassy bell of a mantle over eight long, slender arms. In life almost nothing but the eyes and gut would be visible.

hotspots.label: Mantle
hotspots.text: The mantle is gelatinous and nearly colourless. In adults it reaches about 11 cm long; in brooding females it holds the eggs.

hotspots.label: Arms
hotspots.text: The upper three pairs of arms are about as long as the mantle in juveniles and two to three times longer in adults; the lowest pair is slightly shorter.

hotspots.label: Suckers
hotspots.text: Its suckers are small, widely spaced and set in a single row along each arm.

senses.lede: The one organ a transparent animal cannot hide is its eye — and the glass octopus's eyes seem shaped around that problem.

senses.name: Elongated eyes
senses.text: Examined in two specimens caught at 200 m, its eyes are cylindrical with the lens in the middle, which narrows their field of view sideways.

senses.name: A smaller shadow
senses.text: The upright shape is argued to minimise the eye's silhouette as seen by a predator looking up from below, at the cost of a wider view.

body.lede: Transparency shapes the whole body, but a few internal features are distinctive.

systems.title: Glass tissues
systems.text: Its body is transparent, gelatinous and almost colourless, so that in open water mainly the compact eyes and digestive organs stand out.

systems.title: A mating arm
systems.text: In males the third left arm is modified as a hectocotylus, which delivers sperm to the female and can detach during mating.

mind.lede: Its behaviour is almost unknown; most records come from nets and from the stomachs of whales.

studies.title: Found inside a whale
studies.text: Beaks of glass octopuses were among the remains in the stomach of a northern bottlenose whale stranded on the Danish island of Tåsinge in 1997.

studies.title: Filmed alive
studies.text: A remotely operated vehicle exploring seamounts near the Phoenix Islands filmed two living glass octopuses, one at 680 m.

survival.lede: In open water there is nowhere to hide, so the glass octopus hides in plain sight.

tactics.title: Transparency
tactics.text: Scientists think its near-transparency is largely a defence, making it hard for predators to spot and helping it approach prey.

tactics.title: Shadow-shrinking eyes
tactics.text: Narrow, upright eyes may cast less of a silhouette against the faint light from above.

life.lede: The glass octopus carries its young inside its own body until they hatch.

stages.name: Brooded egg
stages.text: The female broods hundreds of eggs, each about 4 mm long, inside her mantle cavity.

stages.name: Paralarva
stages.text: Newborn young have a mantle about 2.2 mm long. The mother dies soon after they are born, leaving them to fend for themselves.

stages.name: Growing deeper
stages.text: Tiny young live in the upper layers; as they grow, they move away from the surface into deeper water.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults reach about 11 cm in mantle length and up to 45 cm overall, living in the dim twilight and midnight zones.
